cards.q: What is the Big O of a loop `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)` containing `for (int j = 0; j < 10; ++j)`?
cards.a:
O(n)

The inner loop always runs 10 times, a constant. 10n steps is O(n).

cards.q: A function does `for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2)` and, inside, `for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j)`. What is its complexity?
cards.a:
O(n log n)

The outer loop runs about log₂ n times and the inner one n times per outer iteration.

cards.q: Which is true of 5n² + 1000n + 7?
cards.a:
It is O(n²) and also Θ(n²)

For large n the n² term dominates. It is also O(n³), since Big O is only an upper bound, but Θ(n²) is the tight answer.

cards.q: Doubling n makes a function take about 4 times as long. What is its likely growth class?
cards.a:
O(n²)

2² = 4, so the time grows with the square of n.

cards.q: Why is summing a std::vector usually much faster than summing a std::list of the same length?
cards.a:
Its elements are contiguous, so the cache serves the reads

Both are O(n), but the list's nodes are scattered, so many reads wait for main memory, while the vector's neighbours arrive with each cache line and the prefetcher keeps up.

cards.q: Why print the result of a computation you are timing?
cards.a:
So the optimiser cannot remove the computation as unused

If the result is never used, the compiler may skip the work entirely.

cards.q: A dynamic array grows its capacity by 1.5× when full. What is the amortised cost of push_back?
cards.a:
O(1)

Any constant growth factor above 1 keeps the total copying proportional to n.

cards.q: Why does erasing the first element of a std::vector take O(n)?
cards.a:
Every other element shifts one place to the left

The elements must stay contiguous, so they all move down by one.

cards.q: You hold a reference to v[2] and then call v.push_back(x). Is the reference still safe to use?
cards.a:
Only if the push did not reallocate

Reallocation moves the elements to a new block, leaving old references dangling. If capacity was reserved first, no reallocation happens.

cards.q: What does it cost to reach the 500th node of a singly linked list?
cards.a:
O(500): follow 500 links from the head

There is no indexing: every node must be visited on the way.

cards.q: What does a sentinel node in a doubly linked list buy you?
cards.a:
No special cases for the ends or an empty list

Every real node always has real neighbours, so insertion and removal use the same pointer updates everywhere.

cards.q: Why can a destructor that relies on unique_ptr chains crash for a very long list?
cards.a:
The destructors recurse once per node and overflow the stack

Each node's destruction calls the next one's destructor. Unlinking nodes one at a time in a loop keeps the stack depth constant.

cards.q: Which structure suits an undo feature?
cards.a:
A stack: the most recent action is undone first

Undo reverses actions newest first, which is LIFO.

cards.q: Why is a std::vector a poor queue?
cards.a:
Removing from the front shifts every remaining element, O(n)

A ring buffer or deque removes from the front in O(1).

cards.q: A ring buffer of capacity 8 has head = 6 and size = 4. Which slot does the next push write to?
cards.a:
2

(6 + 4) % 8 = 2: the queue occupies slots 6, 7, 0, 1, so the next free slot is 2.

cards.q: A sorted vector has 1,000,000 elements. About how many comparisons does binary search need at most?
cards.a:
20

Each comparison halves the range: 2^20 is just over a million.

cards.q: Why compute mid as lo + (hi - lo) / 2?
cards.a:
(lo + hi) can overflow when both are large

hi - lo always fits, so lo + (hi - lo) / 2 stays in range.

cards.q: In {1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 8}, what are the lower and upper bounds of 3?
cards.a:
1 and 4

The first element >= 3 is at index 1; the first element > 3 is the 5 at index 4. The 3s occupy [1, 4).

cards.q: When can you binary search on the answer?
cards.a:
When the check ok(x) is monotonic in x

Monotonic means once ok(x) is true it stays true for every larger x, which is what lets each check throw away half of the candidates.

cards.q: Which property is required (not just desirable) of a hash function?
cards.a:
Equal keys always produce equal hashes

If equal keys could hash differently, lookups would search the wrong bucket. Different keys sharing a hash is allowed.

cards.q: Why is hashing a point as hash(x) ^ hash(y) a poor choice?
cards.a:
(1, 2) and (2, 1) collide, and x == y gives 0

XOR is symmetric and cancels equal values, so structured keys collide a lot.

cards.q: With 365 buckets, about how many random keys until the first collision is likely?
cards.a:
about 23

The birthday paradox: about the square root of the bucket count.

cards.q: A chained hash table has 1,000 buckets and 3,000 entries, with a good hash. What is the expected chain length?
cards.a:
3

The load factor n / m = 3000 / 1000 = 3.

cards.q: Why does every entry move to a different bucket (in general) during a rehash?
cards.a:
The bucket is hash % bucketCount, and the count changed

The hash stays the same, but taking it modulo a new count gives a new bucket.

cards.q: Why does doubling the buckets when the table is full keep insert at amortised O(1)?
cards.a:
All the rehashes together cost O(n)

Each rehash costs O(n), but they happen at sizes 8, 16, 32, ..., which sum to less than 2n, like a growing vector.

cards.q: In linear probing, why can't erase simply mark the slot empty?
cards.a:
Searches stop at the gap and miss later keys

A key that was pushed past this slot is found by probing through it. Searches stop at the first empty slot, so a hole breaks every probe sequence that ran through it.

cards.q: An open-addressing table has load factor 0.9. What happens?
cards.a:
Misses and inserts take about 50 probes each

With linear probing, probe counts grow like 1/(1-α)²; real tables rehash well before this.

cards.q: Why do many fast hash tables prefer linear probing despite primary clustering?
cards.a:
Neighbouring slots share cache lines

A few extra probes in the same cache line cost almost nothing: memory access, not probe count, dominates the cost on modern hardware.

cards.q: You must repeatedly find the first appointment after a given time. Which container fits?
cards.a:
std::map, using lower_bound

Hash tables cannot answer "next bigger"; ordered containers (or a sorted vector) can, in O(log n).

cards.q: A dictionary of 200,000 words is loaded once and then checked millions of times. Which is a strong choice?
cards.a:
A sorted std::vector with binary search, or a hash set

The data does not change, so a contiguous sorted vector or a hash set gives fast lookups.

cards.q: Why does the longest-consecutive-run algorithm only start counting at x when x - 1 is absent?
cards.a:
So each run is counted once, from its start

Counting from every element would recount long runs again and again, giving O(n²); starting only at run starts keeps the total work O(n).

cards.q: How many inversions does {3, 1, 2} have?
cards.a:
2

(3, 1) and (3, 2) are out of order; (1, 2) is fine.

cards.q: On an already sorted array of n elements, how much work does insertion sort do?
cards.a:
O(n)

Each element is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put. Insertion sort does n plus the number of inversions, and a sorted array has none.

cards.q: Why must a comparator use < rather than <=?
cards.a:
less(a, a) must be false, and <= breaks that

The sort requires a strict weak ordering. With <=, equal elements each claim to be less than the other, which can make std::sort misbehave or crash.

cards.q: What is the recurrence for merge sort?
cards.a:
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)

Two half-size subproblems, plus a linear merge.

cards.q: Which is true of merge sort?
cards.a:
It is stable and always O(n log n)

Taking from the left on ties keeps it stable. The price is a buffer: merging arrays needs O(n) extra memory.

cards.q: Why can no comparison sort beat Ω(n log n) in the worst case?
cards.a:
It must tell apart n! orders, 2 outcomes per comparison

c yes/no comparisons distinguish at most 2^c orderings, and log₂(n!) grows like n log n, so that many comparisons are needed.

cards.q: When does quicksort with "last element as pivot" take O(n²)?
cards.a:
On input that is already sorted (or reversed)

Each partition then splits off just one element, so there are n levels of O(n) work.

cards.q: What does three-way partitioning fix?
cards.a:
Slowness on many equal elements

Equal elements are gathered in the middle and never touched again, so arrays full of duplicates no longer degrade quicksort.

cards.q: Why recurse on the smaller side and loop on the larger one?
cards.a:
It keeps the stack depth at O(log n)

Each recursive call handles at most half of the current range, so the stack cannot overflow (the time can still be O(n²)).

cards.q: What does std::nth_element(b, b + k, e) guarantee?
cards.a:
b + k holds the element sorting would put there

Everything before it is no larger and everything after no smaller, but neither side is sorted. It is quickselect: expected O(n).

cards.q: In an array-stored heap, where are the children of the node at index 5?
Why is building a heap bottom-up O(n) rather than O(n log n)?
cards.a:
Most nodes are near the bottom, where sifts are short

Half the nodes are leaves, a quarter move at most one level, and so on, so the total work sums to less than n.

cards.q: How do you find the 10 largest values in a stream of a billion numbers?
cards.a:
Keep a min-heap of the 10 largest so far

Whenever the heap holds 11, pop its top: the smallest of the current top values, the one to throw out.

cards.q: Why does LSD radix sort need a stable sort for each digit?
cards.a:
To keep the order earlier passes made

Keys that tie on the current digit must stay in the order the previous, less significant passes produced.

cards.q: Counting sort on n = 1,000 values whose keys range up to k = 1,000,000,000 is...
cards.a:
A poor choice: O(n + k)

O(n + k) is dominated by the billion counters. Counting sort only pays off when k is not much bigger than n; radix sort splits such keys into small digits instead.

cards.q: How many counting-sort passes does a base-256 radix sort make over 64-bit unsigned integers?
cards.a:
8

One pass per byte: 64 / 8 = 8.

cards.q: What is the in-order traversal of a tree with root 2, left child 1 and right child 3?
cards.a:
1 2 3

Left subtree, node, right subtree.

cards.q: Which traversal suits deleting every node of a tree safely?
cards.a:
post-order

Children are handled before their parent, so no node is deleted while its children still need it.

cards.q: Which data structure does level-order traversal use?
cards.a:
a queue

First in, first out: nodes are visited in the order they were discovered, level by level.

cards.q: In a BST, where is the smallest key?
cards.a:
At the end of the path that always goes left from the root

Every left step goes to smaller keys; the node with no left child is the minimum.

cards.q: Deleting a node with two children replaces its key with...
cards.a:
Its in-order successor's key

The successor, the smallest key in the right subtree, fits between the left and right subtrees and has at most one child itself.

cards.q: Keys 1, 2, 3, ..., 1000 are inserted into a plain BST in that order. What is its height?
cards.a:
999

Each key becomes the right child of the previous one: a linked list.

cards.q: Which balance factors are allowed in an AVL tree?
cards.a:
-1, 0 and +1

The two subtrees of every node may differ in height by at most one.

cards.q: A node has balance +2 and its left child has balance -1. What fixes it?
cards.a:
Rotate the child left, then the node right

This is the left-right case: the double rotation straightens the zig-zag first.

cards.q: Why does a rotation keep the tree a valid binary search tree?
cards.a:
It keeps the in-order sequence of keys the same

A x B y C reads the same before and after a rotation at y.

cards.q: What is the lowest set bit of 12 (binary 1100)?
cards.a:
4

12 & -12 = 4: the rightmost 1 is in the 4s place.

cards.q: Why can't a Fenwick tree answer range-minimum queries the way it answers range sums?
cards.a:
A minimum cannot be subtracted away

A range sum is prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1). The prefix trick needs an inverse operation, which min does not have.

cards.q: In a segment tree for range sums, what should a query return for a segment that does not overlap [l, r]?
cards.a:
0

The identity of addition, so it does not change the combined result.

cards.q: What does find(x) return?
cards.a:
The root of x's tree, which represents its whole set

Two elements are in the same set exactly when they have the same root.

cards.q: What does union by size do?
cards.a:
Attaches the smaller tree's root under the larger tree's root

A node only gets deeper when its tree at least doubles, so depths stay O(log n).

cards.q: unite(a, b) returns false because a and b are already connected. In a graph built edge by edge, what does that tell you?
cards.a:
The edge (a, b) closes a cycle

There was already a path between a and b; the new edge makes a second one.

cards.q: Why does BFS find shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
cards.a:
It reaches vertices in order of distance

The queue processes all vertices at distance d before any at distance d + 1, so the first visit is along a shortest path.

cards.q: A road network has 1,000,000 junctions and about 2,500,000 roads. Which representation?
cards.a:
adjacency lists

A matrix would need 10^12 entries; adjacency lists need memory proportional to V + E.

cards.q: When should BFS mark a vertex as visited?
cards.a:
When it is pushed onto the queue

Marking on push stops the same vertex being queued several times.

cards.q: In DFS cycle detection on a directed graph, which edge reveals a cycle?
cards.a:
An edge to a grey vertex, one still on the current DFS path

An edge to a finished vertex can occur without a cycle, as in a diamond shape.

cards.q: Kahn's algorithm stops with some vertices never output. What does that mean?
cards.a:
The graph has a cycle among the remaining vertices

Vertices on a cycle wait for each other, so their in-degrees never reach 0.

cards.q: Why can longest paths be found quickly in a DAG but not in general graphs?
cards.a:
In topological order, values are final before use

With no cycles, no later vertex can improve an earlier one, so one pass in topological order is enough.

cards.q: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm finalise the vertex with the smallest tentative distance?
cards.a:
With no negative weights, no other route is shorter

Any other route to it passes through a vertex at least as far away. This is exactly the step that negative weights break.

cards.q: A popped heap entry (d, u) has d > dist[u]. What should Dijkstra do?
cards.a:
Skip it: the entry is out of date

A better distance for u was found after this entry was pushed. That is lazy deletion: stale entries are simply ignored.

cards.q: Bellman-Ford still improves a distance on its V-th pass. What does that mean?
cards.a:
A negative cycle is reachable

Without negative cycles, all shortest paths are settled after V - 1 passes; an improvement after that comes from a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source.

cards.q: Why does a minimum spanning tree never contain a cycle?
cards.a:
Dropping a cycle's costliest edge is cheaper

Removing the most expensive edge of a cycle keeps everything connected and lowers the cost.

cards.q: In Kruskal's algorithm, what does union-find decide?
cards.a:
Whether an edge would close a cycle

It tells whether the edge's two ends are already connected; `unite(a, b)` returning false means they are in the same tree.

cards.q: How does Prim's priority differ from Dijkstra's?
cards.a:
It is one edge's cost, not a path length

A vertex's priority in Prim is the cost of the single edge attaching it to the tree; Dijkstra uses the total distance from the start.

cards.q: What does A* use as the priority of a vertex?
cards.a:
f(n) = g(n) + h(n)

The estimated cost of the cheapest path through n.

cards.q: Which heuristic is admissible for a grid with 4-direction moves costing at least 1?
cards.a:
Manhattan distance

It never overestimates: any 4-direction path needs at least dx + dy steps.

cards.q: What happens with h(n) = 0 for every vertex?
cards.a:
A* behaves exactly like Dijkstra's algorithm

With no estimate, the priority is just the cost so far.

cards.q: For interval scheduling with one room, which greedy rule always gives the most meetings?
cards.a:
earliest finish first

Finishing early leaves the most room for everything else; the exchange argument proves it.

cards.q: With coins 1, 3 and 4, what does "largest coin first" pay for 6?
cards.a:
4 + 1 + 1

Greedy takes three coins, though 3 + 3 uses two: a greedy choice can block a better combination, so this coin system needs dynamic programming.

cards.q: In Huffman coding, which two items are merged at each step?
cards.a:
the two least frequent

Merging the rarest items pushes them deepest, so they get the longest codes.

cards.q: What two properties make a problem suitable for dynamic programming?
cards.a:
optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems

Recursion alone is not enough: DP pays off when the same subproblems repeat.

cards.q: What is the difference between memoisation and tabulation?
cards.a:
Recursion plus a cache, versus a loop over a table

Memoisation keeps the recursion and caches results; tabulation fills a table iteratively in an order that respects the dependencies. Both solve each subproblem once.

cards.q: In the "ways to make change" loop, why are the coins in the outer loop?
cards.a:
So each combination is counted only once

With the amounts outside, 1 + 3 and 3 + 1 would be counted as different ways; coins outside fix one order.

cards.q: Why does the one-row 0/1 knapsack loop over capacities from high to low?
cards.a:
So best[w - weight] still holds the previous item's row, and the item is counted at most once

Going upwards would reuse the current item: that is the unbounded knapsack.

cards.q: What is the edit distance between "flaw" and "lawn"?
cards.a:
2

Delete the f and insert an n at the end.

cards.q: In the O(n log n) longest-increasing-subsequence method, what does tails[k] hold?
cards.a:
The smallest end of a run of length k + 1

tails[k] is the smallest last value of any increasing subsequence of length k + 1 so far. Keeping the ends small leaves the most room for later values to extend them.

cards.q: Why is looking up a word of length L in a trie O(L), regardless of how many words it holds?
cards.a:
It follows one edge per character

The lookup walks from the root one character at a time, and the number of stored words does not affect the length of that path.

cards.q: What is the prefix function of "aabaa"?
cards.a:
0 1 0 1 2

For "aabaa" the longest border is "aa" (length 2); for "aab" there is none.

cards.q: What makes KMP linear even though it has a loop inside a loop?
cards.a:
Inner steps total at most n over the run

The matched length k rises by at most one per text character, and each inner step lowers it. This is amortised analysis: count the total work over the whole run.

cards.q: What are the three steps inside a backtracking loop?
cards.a:
choose, explore, unchoose

Apply a choice, recurse, then undo it so the next choice starts from the same state.

cards.q: How does the N-queens solver check diagonals in O(1)?
cards.a:
With arrays indexed by row + col and row - col

Squares on one diagonal share row + col, and on the other row - col, so one boolean array per direction records whether a queen is there.

cards.q: What does branch and bound add to backtracking?
cards.a:
Pruning branches that cannot beat the best

It abandons partial solutions whose best possible outcome cannot beat the best solution found so far, which prunes large parts of the search tree.
